title: Are Fake Citations a Form of Reward Hacking? A Pre-Registered Study of Post-Training and Citation Cues
summary: Post-trained language models fabricate citations at high rates. We ask whether that is reward hacking: scoring well on a proxy for scholarship while doing worse on what it stands for. We ran four pre-registered experiments on 900 frozen questions (US federal case law, computationally adjacent scientific literature, and medical literature) across twelve open-weights checkpoints covering four post-training stages of three model families, then refit on fifteen. The clearest result holds the weights fixed and changes only the prompt. Asking for citations raises fabrication sharply in post-trained checkpoints and not in base ones: a 47.8-point interaction on twelve checkpoints (Holm-adjusted p = 2e-34) and 41.5 points on fifteen, in all three domains. A length-matched control separates the citation cue from a demand for a longer answer, so the effect is specific to citations, not verbosity. Post-training also raises fabrication overall, from 4.8% to 56.7%, but our registered prediction that it would rise most where fabrication is most tempting did not hold. A preference model trained only on surface citation features prefers post-trained output 86% of the time, and holding citation count fixed shows it rewards quantity. Our answer: possibly, but not proven. Post-trained models produce fabricated citations at far higher rates when asked for sources, and a naive evaluator that counts sources without checking them would prefer their output for citing more. But the targeted pattern we registered did not appear, and plain instruction-following could explain the same results. Proving that the reward causes fabrication needs an experiment that changes the reward during training, which this study does not do. Pre-registration: doi:10.17605/OSF.IO/S53HY. Code and data: https://github.com/zainnab-sparq/citation-reward-hacking

title: Multi-Estimate Elicitation Does Not Uniformly Debias Language Model Judgments
summary: Does eliciting five weighted estimates within a single response change how a language model responds to information? Across anchoring, hindsight, base-rate, conjunction, and status-quo/default tasks, we compare direct numerical answers with a multi-estimate response format, contrasting source framings, explicitly random cues, and probability-consistency constraints. We evaluate three completed configurations--gpt-6.1-sol, claude-sonnet-5.5, and Qwen3-8B (reasoning disabled, analyzed descriptively). In the first two configurations, direct elicitation yielded near-zero irrelevant-anchor indices and status-quo effects, while remaining responsive to informative sources and informed advice. Of 23 preregistered confirmatory tests, six rejected after Holm adjustment; however, all six absolute point estimates fell below their prespecified smallest effect sizes of interest without establishing equivalence. Moreover, while separate versus joint elicitation shifted conjunction judgments, interpretation is constrained by between-call noise. Ultimately, multi-estimate elicitation failed to produce uniform debiasing or response attenuation across tasks and models, though post hoc correlations between candidate spread and anchoring error motivate independent predictive validation. Materials: https://github.com/asj252/llm-judgment-studies

title: Step-dLLM: Adaptive Step-aware Sparse Attention for Efficient Diffusion LLM Inference
summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate tokens in parallel via iterative denoising, but their bidirectional attention prevents the KV caching used by autoregressive models and recomputes the full attention map at every step, incurring quadratic per-step cost. Existing sparse attention methods for dLLMs construct a sparse mask after an initial full-attention warm-up and reuse it for the remaining steps, while allocating the sparsity budget uniformly across heads. We argue both choices ignore key structural properties of attention in dLLMs: empirically, attention patterns are only locally consistent across steps and shift abruptly at certain transitions, and different heads concentrate their attention mass to very different extents. To this end, we design Step-dLLM, which periodically refreshes a block-sparse mask at anchor steps along the denoising trajectory and reuses it within each locally consistent interval, while employing a head-adaptive global budget that more aggressively compresses heads with concentrated attention. Backed by a fused IO-aware Triton kernel for block-sparse attention, Step-dLLM applies to pre-trained LLaDA-1.5 and Dream-7B-Instruct without retraining, achieving a 2.78x end-to-end speedup over dense FlashAttention on LLaDA-1.5 at 8K context with 256 denoising steps and 90% sparsity, while improving the accuracy-latency trade-off over prior sparse-attention methods.

title: Is Newborn Wiring Special? Separating Wiring from Weight Placement in Connectome Reservoirs
summary: Reservoir computing offers a way to study the brain's wiring before it is even trained. The recurrent network remains fixed, while only a linear readout is trained. The human connectome is found to perform better than randomly rewired versions of itself, suggesting that biological wiring is special. To understand the source of this advantage, a mathematical graph-theoretic decomposition is introduced. Rewiring a weighted network changes both the regions that are connected and the weights assigned to those connections. The observed advantage therefore combines an effect of wiring with an effect of weight placement. These effects are separated by averaging the wiring term over the null model's weight rule, as a single draw introduces about one z-unit of noise. Adult and infant connectomes are then considered separately. In adult Human Connectome Project graphs, weight placement explains most of the reported effect, leaving a small but consistent wiring effect. Across the full dHCP release, a large wiring effect is found at every measured gestational age at birth, while gestational age explains almost none of its variance. The connectomes are also compared with non-brain networks. A Watts-Strogatz graph matched in size, edge count, weights, and strength performs as well as or better than the connectome. The newborn connectome's advantage is therefore real across all measured gestational ages, but it is not unique to the brain. The same separation can be applied whenever a weighted network is compared with rewired nulls.

title: The Verifier Is Part of the Simulator: Evidence-View Gaming in Agentic Equation Discovery
summary: A growing number of agentic pipelines search for governing equations: an agent proposes laws and a verifier checks them against simulated trajectories. The verifier sees only a numerical summary: integrals against test functions on a time grid. That summary carries its own discretization error, making the verifier part of the simulator. We freeze the trajectory, candidate library, verifier and thresholds, leaving the agent one move: which permitted summary to admit. Without scores or language models, finer time grids reduce numerical discrepancies and false library rejections. On PDEBench, the verifier instead accepts equations missing diffusion on score-selected summaries. Maximizing a public score rewarding decisive verdicts and larger mismatches when rejecting the library wrongly rejects all 1,500 in-library cases; retrospectively retuning score constants on a separate bank reduces errors to 13/180 at best. We call this evidence-view gaming: reward hacking by choice of permitted summary. In single-turn forced-choice tests, Claude models rarely choose summaries giving wrong verdicts when asked to be accurate, but often do so when asked to maximize the score or report missing physics. In separate trust prompts, they often rank those harmful summaries least trustworthy. Requiring several summaries to agree reduces errors but often withholds a verdict and performs worse than a fixed fine view on PDEBench: a safeguard, not a certificate. Evidence chosen after its verdict is known cannot alone authorize a claim.

title: VoirDire: Counterfactual Calibration for Reliable LLM-as-a-Judge Aggregation
summary: LLM-as-a-judge systems often aggregate multiple judges to improve evaluation reliability. However, judge agreement can reflect shared biases toward verbosity, formatting, or fluency rather than the intended evaluation target. Addressing these shared biases is challenging because observational judge outputs alone cannot distinguish agreement driven by target quality from agreement driven by nuisance attributes. We introduce VoirDire, an intervention-calibrated aggregation method for LLM-judge panels. VoirDire applies controlled interventions that vary specified surface attributes while aiming to preserve the evaluation target; it then uses paired changes in judge scores to identify nuisance-sensitive directions. It attenuates these directions and selects aggregation weights that retain variation across items while penalizing sensitivity to the interventions, making the final consensus less dependent on superficial features. We show theoretically that observational judge outputs alone cannot identify which shared direction is target-relevant, while paired interventions provide the contrast needed to identify nuisance-sensitive variation. We evaluate VoirDire on 12 datasets spanning continuous scoring, binary classification, and pairwise preference. Compared with the existing LLM-judge aggregation baselines, VoirDire reduces MAE by up to 26.8% on continuous-score tasks and improves accuracy by up to 5.3 percentage points on binary and preference tasks. These findings suggest that counterfactual interventions provide an additional means of improving the reliability and controllability of LLM-based evaluation beyond merely relying on observed judge agreement.

title: The Long Con on the Web: Earn-then-Exploit Fraud Attacks against Coding Agents
summary: Coding agents increasingly operate with web access and high privileges, creating a new attack surface where web fraud can directly target autonomous agents. Existing studies mainly focus on malicious links, prompt injection, and interface deception, while content-level web fraud against agents and the amplification of attacks through agent trust remain underexplored. In this paper, we present EtE (Earn-then-Exploit), a web fraud attack framework against coding agents, in which a malicious website first provides multiple rounds of genuinely verifiable assistance to establish trust and then introduces task-related instructions that cross intended operational boundaries. To systematically evaluate its effectiveness, we construct 56 organizational environments (8 task contexts x 7 attack consequences) and evaluate three representative coding agents. EtE achieves an average scene-level attack success rate of 71.4%, including 85.7% on Codex-GPT-5.5, 67.9% on ZCode-GLM-5.3-Flash, and 60.7% on QwenCode-Qwen3.7-Plus, significantly outperforming all injection-based baselines. More importantly, our experiments reveal that coding agents exhibit trust-like behavioral reliance on previously helpful Web sources, and that such accumulated credibility significantly increases their susceptibility to subsequent malicious instructions. Based on this finding, we propose action-authorization separation (AAS), which prevents web content from directly authorizing privileged actions and reduces the attack success rate to 0% while preserving 100% task completion, outperforming all evaluated defense baselines.

title: Model-Based Learning of Latent Euclidean Embedding from Relational Data
summary: Visualizing and interpreting the dependence structure in relational data often benefits from geometric representations via low-dimensional Euclidean embeddings. However, existing approaches are typically restricted to specific response types, rely on burdensome high-dimensional nonconvex optimization, or lack uniform theoretical guarantees for simultaneous coordinate recovery. To address these limitations, we introduce a unified, distance-based latent space framework for both unipartite and bipartite relational data---accommodating continuous, binary, ordinal, and count-valued observations---via a modular two-stage procedure that decouples signal estimation from geometric recovery. First, we estimate the low-rank signal matrix using spectral denoising. For models with nonlinear link functions, we further apply one-step row- and column-wise refinement to achieve uniform entrywise accuracy. Second, we recover the latent configurations through direct spectral analysis for unipartite data and a low-dimensional alignment optimization for bipartite data. We establish uniform recovery guarantees that characterize the propagation of error from signal estimation to the embedding space. To illustrate the scalability and interpretability of our approach, we apply the proposed method to two real-world datasets: a statistician citation network and European Parliament voting records.

title: CuPH: Parallel Cubical Persistent Homology via Level-Synchronous Component Tracking
summary: Persistent homology (PH) is a mathematically principled multi-scale topological descriptor of shape and connectivity in data. It is widely applied in image classification, segmentation, and shape analysis across medical and aerial imaging, providing structural information that pixel-wise deep learning may overlook. Standard cubical PH decomposes an image into cubical cells (vertices, edges, and squares) and reduces them sequentially in filtration order. This sequential reduction has $Θ(n)$ parallel depth for an $n$-pixel image, limiting within-image GPU parallelism and constraining its use in topology-aware deep learning. We introduce CuPH, a GPU-based parallel algorithm for computing cubical PH on 2D images that operates directly on pixels rather than cubical cells. CuPH buckets pixels by filtration values, activates them with a level-synchronous sweep, and tracks connected components with a lock-free union-find method. We prove that CuPH produces persistence diagrams identical to standard cubical PH on integer inputs, with a stability bound for floating-point inputs. CuPH reduces parallel depth from $Θ(n)$ to $O(L\log n)$ for an image with $L$ intensity levels. We implement the level sweep as a single CUDA kernel, eliminating cross-level kernel-launch overhead. Empirically, CuPH is $18.6$--$99.6\times$ faster than the existing GPU baseline (CMP). As a drop-in PH backend, CuPH accelerates topology-aware classification ($4.2$--$16.7\times$) and segmentation ($8.3$--$44\times$) while preserving accuracy. It also enables computing full-image PH losses on high-resolution images, improving segmentation Dice by $2.2$--$4.6$ points over patch-local PH baselines and accelerating training by $25$--$31\times$.

title: The Blind Spots of Detection: Adversarial Perturbation Attacks against Watchdogs in Distributed LLM Inference
summary: Decentralizing large language model (LLM) inference across untrusted Web nodes requires robust verification to ensure computational integrity. Existing activation-based verification and detection mechanisms validate intermediate outputs against reference values, permitting bounded numerical deviations to accommodate benign cross-hardware discrepancies. However, a critical security question remains: what can a malicious worker achieve while operating within these tolerance bounds? In this work, we introduce Hush-Up, a stealthy availability attack against distributed LLM inference, where a single malicious worker halts generation while evading attribution. The attacker first profiles its local execution to model an empirical bound of benign hardware errors. Using this error bound as a feasibility constraint, the attacker optimizes an adversarial perturbation on its output activations to maximize the final-layer probability of the end-of-sequence (EOS) token, i.e., to hush up the model. Across diverse models and benchmarks, Hush-Up effectively forces premature generation termination and collapses model capabilities. Furthermore, the attack hushes up the watchdogs themselves: existing defenses often fail to detect the sabotage entirely or falsely attribute the amplified downstream anomalies to honest workers. Our findings expose a fundamental gap between local numerical verification and end-to-end accountability: perturbations too small to indict a worker locally can nevertheless be powerful enough to break distributed inference globally.

title: Zeroth-Order Policy Optimization for Scheduling in Queueing Networks
summary: Reinforcement learning in queueing network scheduling presents significant challenges because of the countably infinite state space and the high stochasticity in transitions. In this paper, we propose zeroth-order policy optimization algorithms that are easy to implement and rely solely on estimates of the average cost, a single scalar quantity, without requiring the estimation of value or advantage functions. Our analysis focuses on back-pressure guarded policies and establishes uniform smoothness of the average cost objective with respect to the policy parameters. Building on this property, we establish finite-time convergence guarantees to an $ε$-stationary policy for the proposed algorithms. Numerical experiments on multiple queueing networks, including systems beyond classical exponential service distribution, demonstrate competitive performance, outperforming gradient-based RL methods like PPO and traditional queueing baselines.

title: ArSciKids: Arabic Curriculum-Aligned Datasets for Scientific Experiment and Multiple-Choice Question Generation in Primary Education
summary: Despite growing interest in Arabic natural language processing, curriculum-aligned educational resources remain scarce compared with English, and few public datasets for Arabic curriculum content with structured, generation-ready annotations are available, particularly for primary-school science. We introduce ArSciKids, a collection of two Arabic datasets designed for curriculum-aligned educational content generation: (1) a scientific-experiments dataset containing 999 manually curated records from official primary-school science textbooks in Saudi Arabia, Syria, and Jordan, and (2) an assessment-question dataset containing 2,167 multiple-choice questions collected from the Saudi Manhaji educational platform. The experiment records are structured with titles, objectives, tools, procedures, observations, conclusions, keywords, and grade levels, while the assessment records contain lesson references, questions, four answer options, correct answers, and explanations. Both datasets cover grades 1-6 and consist of real-life Arabic educational content rather than machine-translated or synthetically generated material. We assess the usefulness of these resources for generation by fine-tuning ten open models spanning sub-billion to several-billion parameter scales using LoRA. Models are evaluated using automatic metrics, including ROUGE and BLEU, and answer accuracy for multiple-choice generation. Moreover, we evaluate the results using a five-criterion human evaluation protocol. The results show substantial differences across model scales and tasks. ArSciKids will be publicly available, and we hope that it provides a manually curated, structured foundation for research on Arabic educational NLP, curriculum-aware generation, and low-resource language modeling.

title: Skill++: Towards Lifelong Agents via Routing-Aware Skill Refinement
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents extend their capabilities with skills, each with a name, a description, and a body. Under progressive disclosure, an LLM router selects skills by name and description alone and loads only the selected bodies. Skill libraries grow continually as users and agents add new skills. Because the router relies on this metadata, a similar new skill can displace an earlier one, breaking previously correct routing even though the earlier skill and the router are unchanged. This routing interference is aggravated for public skills, whose descriptions may not match their bodies. We formulate the problem as lifelong skill routing, a class-incremental continual learning problem. A solution must keep earlier skills selectable without suppressing new ones. Existing approaches fall short, since continually retraining the router risks catastrophic forgetting and rewriting methods either ignore similar skills or require per-skill feedback. We therefore propose Skill++, which rewrites only the name and description of each incoming skill, without router training or labeled data. The new description states what the body supports, how the skill differs from its closest predecessor, and what related work it excludes. As a library grows to 731 skills over ten sessions, Skill++ selects all required skills for 76.3% of queries, versus 36.4% under the original metadata. Across three benchmarks and five LLM routers, it outperforms all compared approaches, and its gains carry over to the Codex CLI agent harness.

title: ProofPatch: Reviewing Lean Statements and Keeping the Reviews Valid as Formalizations Evolve
summary: The kernel of the Lean proof assistant checks that a proof establishes its statement. Whether the statement says what was intended is left to human reviewers. This is the old problem of validating a specification, and it grows more pressing as language models write formal statements in bulk and agents edit formal developments continuously. We present ProofPatch, a tool that helps reviewers judge Lean statements and keeps their judgments valid while the development changes. A reviewer can ask the kernel targeted questions about a statement, such as whether a hypothesis is needed or whether a counterexample exists. Each decision is stored with fingerprints of the statement as Lean elaborated it and of the definitions it depends on, and any declaration can be pinned so that a patch changing it is blocked, whether a person or an agent built on a large language model (LLM) wrote the patch. Working on elaborated terms rather than source text is the central design choice: notation and formatting changes leave a decision intact, and a changed definition reaches every theorem that uses it. On 229 pairs of consecutive revisions of Mathlib, Lean's mathematics library, ProofPatch sends 118 of 12,898 synthetic decisions back for review. Every text-based alternative misses at least 38 of these or sends back at least 13 times as many. On 1,527 labeled statements, kernel evidence flags unfaithful ones with precision 0.88 to 0.96, and in 344 runs of an LLM agent no change to a pinned statement got through.

title: Governing Equations of Human Sleep Macro-Structure:Symbolic Discovery from 1,106 Nights
summary: Human sleep is organized into a small number of cycles per night: deep sleep dominates early cycles, REM lengthens toward morning, and light sleep clusters at cycle boundaries. These regularities have long been described qualitatively but never distilled into closed-form laws from large-scale data. A total of 1,106 nights (Sleep-EDF 153 + SHHS 953) are segmented into REM-anchored cycles, and four cycle-indexed statistics follow simple closed-form equations: cycle length declines nearly linearly (R^2=0.996), REM duration follows an inverted U (R^2=0.873), deep-sleep (N3) run length decays exponentially (R^2=0.987) with a time constant of 2.94 cycles, consistent with the homeostatic Process S of the two-process model, and light-sleep (N1) run length follows a U shape (R^2=0.956), confirming a "long-short-long" pattern across the night. The laws are reproduced by per-night differentiable fitting (142/142 and 773/773 nights converge), by unconstrained symbolic regression (PySR), and by a 500-night generative synthesizer built from them. Their robustness is established against the two main methodological threats: bootstrap CIs computed by resampling whole nights (1,000 replications) exclude zero for every shape term, and a five-level scan of the REM-merge segmentation threshold preserves every qualitative form. These appear to be the first closed-form laws governing the macro-structure of sleep, distilled and tested across an age-mixed sample (healthy young adults and community-based older adults).

title: Spotting the Artificial: Dialogic Humor Improvisation in Humans and LLMs
summary: We propose a methodology for investigating the differences between natural and synthetic language in a challenging setting: humorous improvisational dialogue. Our experimental setting compares human-produced comedy improvisations with the dialogues generated by LLMs in a multi-agent environment that we designed. The analysis combines automated linguistic measures with manual annotation grounded in Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL). The results show that, although LLMs can create coherent and creative scenes, they often fail to reproduce key characteristics of spontaneous spoken interaction. In addition, LLM-generated interactions display a strong tendency toward politeness and positive evaluations, contrasting with the broader range of attitudes found in human humorous improvisation. Our evidence highlights both the strengths and limitations of current LLMs in modeling dialogic humor and demonstrate the value of integrating linguistic theory with NLP methods for the analysis of machine-generated language

title: Spatial Token Interleaving and Two-Pass BP Decoding for Semantic Image Transmission
summary: Semantic error control coding (SECC) can correct the residual errors of a standard channel code with a foundation model that supplies a prior on the source content, but existing SECC schemes are designed for text. In this paper, we develop SECC for image transmission with spatial token interleaving and a two-pass belief propagation (BP) schedule. At the transmitter, a vector-quantized (VQ) tokenizer converts an image into tokens, which are transmitted in multiple low-density parity-check (LDPC) code blocks of fifth-generation New Radio (5G NR). In raster order, a block that BP fails to decode corrupts consecutive token rows, so the interleaver reorders the tokens such that adjacent tokens are carried by different blocks, without additional transmitted bits. At the receiver, after the first BP pass, token recovery fuses the token probabilities given by BP with the predictions of the autoregressive model Emu3-Gen, and the second BP pass decodes each block again with the fused distributions as priors on the information bits. On Kodak24 at 0.5 channel uses per pixel and a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 0.15 dB, the second pass removes 92% of the token errors left by token recovery, and interleaving reduces the final token error rate by 88%. At medium to high SNR, the proposed receiver exceeds deep joint source--channel coding baselines with the same channel uses by at least 1.2 dB in peak signal-to-noise ratio.

title: E-UDE: A Scientific Machine Learning Model for Malware Propagation Dynamics
summary: Understanding the malware propagation dynamics over the Internet is crucial for effectively controlling its spread. Existing mechanistic and data-driven models in the context of malware propagation dynamics, have some issues with either interpretability or predictive accuracy. This study presents an Enhanced Universal Differential Equation (E-UDE) framework that explicitly incorporates more detailed key factors that influence malware propagation. Evaluation on real-world malware propagation data shows that the E-UDE achieves the best overall performance, attaining an overall RMSE of 783.70 and MAE of 421.65. Compared with the Classical ODE and the UDE models, the proposed approach reduces RMSE by approximately 66 percent and 39 percent, respectively. Its robustness to predictive capability is further evaluated. In this experiment, the E-UDE achieves a Test RMSE of 634.6, a Test MAE of 419.3, and a Test Correlation of 0.964. The E-UDE maintains relatively stable prediction performance as the noise level increases, showing limited degradation compared with the baseline models. Furthermore, this E-UDE model enables us to perform several scenario analyses under different cybersecurity scenarios, providing a useful framework for better understanding the effective control factors. To study the wide applicability of the E-UDE framework, the model performance is assessed by two different datasets, namely, Code Red dataset and Witty Worm dataset.

title: STLT: A Novel System for Energy-Aware Distributed Inference in the Edge-Cloud-Space Continuum
summary: Low Earth Orbit satellites are pivotal for Earth observation tasks such as wildfire detection, capturing imagery for analysis by Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). On-board analysis reduces downlink volume, but severe energy constraints force a trade-off between computation and data transmission. Splitting the DNN between satellite and ground turns this balance into a design choice, where the split point determines combined computation and downlink energy. Existing approaches typically rely on static split-point decisions that fail to account for dynamic space conditions, or on complex algorithms, historical data, or prediction models that introduce significant overhead. To address these shortcomings, we present STLT, a two-stage system for energy-aware distributed inference between LEO satellites and a ground station. First, an offline analyzer characterizes the DNN architecture to identify a set of favorable split points, consequently reducing the search space. Second, an on-board algorithm performs lightweight energy-aware split selection, dynamically choosing from this pre-computed set based on the current state of the environment. We evaluate STLT on a real-world satellite telemetry dataset, showing that it reduces the split-candidate search space by 30.7% on average, lowers decision latency by 25.1% and energy by 27.5% on average, and delivers up to 20.1% more inference tasks than a state-of-the-art satellite-ground co-inference baseline while consuming 8.8% less energy overall.

title: From Apparent Search Gains to Selection Failures: Auditing Test-Time Inference in Structured Workflow Planning
summary: Test-time search can improve structured planning, but when methods differ in prompts, post-processing, and selection, it is unclear what an observed gain should be attributed to. We study this question on DisasterBench, where models compose typed multi-tool workflows, by decomposing inference into three observable stages: whether a correct workflow is discovered, whether it survives structural validation, and whether it is finally selected. Comparing independent sampling, a nominal tree-search configuration, and multi-operator search under controlled inference budgets on two model families, we find that (i) the nominal tree-search configuration realizes non-adaptive complete-workflow sampling, and independent sampling with its expansion prompt reproduces its candidate discovery without constructing a tree; (ii) structural validation never removes the last correct workflow in our evaluated candidate pools, whereas majority voting leaves a discovered correct workflow unselected on 10-19% of tasks per pool, with an audit confirming substantive tool-choice or information-flow errors in 57 of 60 examined cases; and (iii) a tool-specification-aware verifier recovers some of these losses but overturns more correct decisions than it fixes. Our results motivate auditing realized rather than nominal inference pipelines, and reporting discovery, validity, and selection separately.

title: DramaVQA: Probing Detailed Understanding of Ultra-Long TV Dramas
summary: Despite recent progress in long-form video understanding, current benchmarks mostly focus on short clips or hour-scale videos. This leaves a major gap in evaluating ultra-long video understanding, where videos often last tens of hours. To bridge this gap, we introduce DramaVQA, a large-scale benchmark built upon long-form TV dramas. Containing approximately 20K question-answering (QA) pairs, the scale of DramaVQA exceeds previous long-video datasets, such as Video-MME and LVBench, by an order of magnitude. Our benchmark has two main features that make it stand out from existing datasets. First, we establish a scalable, LLM-assisted annotation pipeline that uses multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to generate complex questions, followed by strict human checking to ensure high data quality. Second, DramaVQA introduces a multi-level time structure; queries are designed across different video lengths, with the hardest questions requiring overall understanding across the entire drama. Extensive evaluations show that state-of-the-art MLLMs face major challenges when tested on these very long videos, highlighting the need for agentic AI algorithms capable of managing long-term memory. The project is available at https://github.com/xinyuehuo/DramaVQA

title: Now You See Them, Now You Dont FusionGhost Gait for Occlusion-Robust Gait Recognition with ArabGait dataset
summary: Skeleton-based gait recognition is generally more robust to appearance changes than pixel-based methods, but this robustness depends on stable pose extraction. Clothing variation in gait recognition includes changes in garments, silhouette, and carried items; under Gulf clothing (Kandoora/Abaya), the dominant failure mode shifts from appearance change to lower-limb pose degradation caused by severe occlusion. To study this regime, we introduce ArabGait, a 45-subject indoor multi-view dataset with four walking conditions across three viewpoints, and show that Gulf clothing lowers mean lower-limb confidence from 0.811 to 0.683 and raises lower-limb failure rate from 7.98% to 17.82%, with ankles most affected. We propose FusionGhost-Gait, a fused spatiotemporal architecture that integrates spatial graph blocks and temporal modeling in one residual unit, removes redundant channel projections, and uses compact temporal Ghost kernels as a lightweight regularization mechanism for pose-noisy trajectories while preserving efficient temporal downsampling. On ArabGait cross-clothing evaluation, including Protocol A and Protocol B, FusionGhost-Gait reaches up to 67.91% Rank-1 while remaining compact (108,970- 133,674 parameters and 0.035-0.052 billion floating-point operations (GFLOPs)), achieving more than 65% fewer parameters and 75% lower FLOPs than existing baselines. These results indicate that the proposed model generalizes effectively to challenging Gulf-clothing conditions while remaining lightweight and deployable for surveillance and access-control biometric systems.

title: Where Causal Discovery Breaks on Real Data: Measuring the Assumptions One Property at a Time
summary: Causal discovery is usually evaluated on simulators or on systems whose ground truth follows from physics or design. When it fails on other real data, the failure is attributed to assumptions that may not hold, but which ones fail, and by how much, is rarely measured. We measure the observable properties of the data they bear on, one property at a time, on a real panel. The case study follows 2,901 US public firms over 31 quarters, with 71 types of corporate action from SEC 8-K filings, 11 financial-statement items, and an expert graph over 651 action-state pairs. The panel breaks measurable requirements of discovery: tails that survive winsorisation, balance-sheet items and revenue close to random walks, and interventions too rare to detect effects of a tenth of a standard deviation in 40 of 71 actions. Even so, a marginal test ranks expert-labelled direct above not-direct pairs within each action (AUROC 0.658) better than every null we built, so the panel does carry information about which pairs are direct. Tuned discovery methods, in configurations feasible at this panel size, recover less of it than a simple pairwise cross-correlation when pairs are ranked within each action, and no more when they are ranked within each target, which removes what the target alone predicts. Most direct pairs (132 of 222) involve actions below the support needed for 80% power against a 0.1-SD effect. For flow targets, conditioning on the target's other expert-labelled parents, often filed alongside the action, erodes the marginal discrimination, and most not-direct associations survive it: even with the graph's parent sets supplied, the expected separation does not emerge. For each property, we give a diagnostic computable before any discovery method is run.

title: Editing the Goal: Per-Token SAE Steering and Its Depth Limits in $π_{0.5}$
summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have recovered interpretable, causally relevant features in robot foundation models (RFMs) such as $π_{0.5}$ (arXiv:2603.19183, arXiv:2603.19233). SAE features on individual instruction tokens are less interpretable than timestep-pooled ones (arXiv:2603.19183), and whether they can redirect a robot's goal remains untested. We show that replacing the SAE features of a single goal word with those of an alternative goal word, leaving the instruction text unchanged, steers $π_{0.5}$-LIBERO into completing the alternative task. At layer 0, BatchTopK feature swaps redirect behavior in up to 20/20 rollouts in a scene where random-feature swaps redirect none, with success varying across six scenes in two LIBERO suites and across layers. The effect depends on SAE architecture: word-selected Matryoshka edits largely do not outperform random ones. SAEs are also not required. Adding a fixed difference-in-means vector at twice its natural magnitude redirects 8-10/10 rollouts. Layer-wise activation patching shows that goal-word edits remain effective up to layer 6 for object location and layer 2 for object identity, and up to layer 13 in both cases when patching also covers camera tokens. These results are proof of existence in an RFM in simulation and an initial map of how deep goal-redirecting edits remain effective. Visit https://doubleblind-sae-pi05.github.io for video rollouts.
comment: Accepted to the Science of Physical AI Safety (SPAIS) Workshop at CoRL 2026. 6 pages, 2 figures

title: Boosted Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Solving Homogeneous and Non-Homogeneous Lane-Emden Type Equations
summary: The Lane-Emden Equation is a class of nonlinear differential equations commonly used to model phenomena in astrophysics and mathematical physics, such as stellar structure and thermal behavior in polytropic gas spheres. This study presents a novel hybrid framework that integrates Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) with boosting methods to enhance the accuracy and robustness of solutions for Lane-Emden type differential equations. Standard PINNs leverage physical laws encoded within the loss function, but their predictive performance can be constrained by optimization challenges and approximation errors. To address this, we introduce a post-processing boosting stage where the residual errors from the PINN prediction are modeled using some regression algorithms - including LightGBM, Random Forest, XGBoost, and Support Vector Regression (SVR). The outputs from these boosted models are aggregated to generate a corrected, high-fidelity prediction. The proposed methodology is systematically validated through quantitative metrics and comparative analysis against the standard PINN baseline. The results demonstrate that the boosted PINN framework significantly reduces prediction error, and improves generalization, offering a powerful and flexible approach for solving scientific and engineering problems governed by differential equations.

title: Can agents reliably design therapeutic antibodies?
summary: Recent work has demonstrated agents driving protein design workflows, either through orchestration of specialized tools or direct manipulation of sequences. Yet the fidelity with which agents follow protein design instructions and the factors contributing to their effectiveness remain understudied. We examine agentic antibody design under two settings: when explicit molecular-editing instructions are provided and when agents receive only previously-scored sequences and are prompted to propose improvements. We call the first task-guided and the second black-box design. For the task-guided setting, we curate ten expert-validated affinity-improvement tasks and show that LLM judges closely reproduce programmatic evaluations of instruction following. We then study two augmentations: access to antibody-relevant tools and to previously scored design history. Tools improve instruction following (IF) and sequence space exploration while reducing optimization performance, whereas design history reduces IF but improves optimization performance at the expense of exploration. Finally, we combine taskguided and black-box design within an in silico optimization loop and show that our agentic optimizer performs comparably to an established Bayesian optimization baseline.

title: Designing Informative Actions: Action Construction for Long-Horizon Research Agents
summary: Large language model agents support automated scientific research by connecting literature analysis and planning with experimentation. Evaluating which action an agent selects does not establish which experiment its instruction specifies, because omitted interventions or replication counts leave consequential choices to the executor. We introduce a reading-set framework for evaluating action construction under a common cost rule. Across 30 synthetic states, complete-design requests increase affordable efficiency by 465.98% and 327.91% relative to the action-name baseline in the two model families, respectively. An author-constructed research-action evaluation dataset provides 60 scenarios for complementary judgment evaluation. On this dataset, the scenario-level information-per-cost measure has a mean within-scenario correlation of 0.733 with judgments from 18 human participants. The framework makes design specification and execution ambiguity measurable, providing a reproducible basis for assessing how research agents translate scientific intent into informative, budget-feasible experiments.

title: Learning momenta for Hamiltonian-based models
summary: There has been increasing interest in methodologies that incorporate physics priors into neural network architectures to enhance their modeling capabilities. Among these methodologies, Hamiltonian neural networks (HNNs) and their variants have gained considerable attention. These architectures explicitly encode Hamiltonian mechanics both in their structure and loss function, resulting in desirable properties and additional modeled information. A crucial limitation of HNNs is their reliance on data on the target system's generalized momenta. This severely hampers their applicability when the analytical form of the generalized momenta is unknown, which frequently is the case in real-world applications. The goal of the present work is to develop a general extension of Hamiltonian-based architectures that addresses this issue by simultaneously learning the system's generalized momenta, Hamiltonian structure, and dynamics from data. The proposed architecture learns the generalized momenta when their analytical form is unknown, and only (potentially non-sequential) data on the state and its derivatives is available. A dissipative mass-spring system, a double pendulum, and a rolling disk under nonholonomic constraints are considered as canonical examples to assess the performance of the proposed architecture.

title: 3D Neural Rendering for Automated Ultrasonic Laser Scans
summary: Laser doppler vibrometer (LDV) scans can be used to detect defects and cracks in manufactured parts before they are deployed. This work presents a method for reconstructing the steady-state surface wavefield of a three-dimensional part by combining automated robotic manipulation with neural rendering. A six-degree-of-freedom (6-DOF) robotic manipulator (UFactory xArm6) with an embedded piezoelectric transducer presented an acoustically excited test article to a stationary LDV at a sequence of known orientations, yielding a set of complex-valued 2D scans with poses derived analytically from the arm kinematics rather than from image-based pose estimation. These scans were used to train a novel complex-nerfacto model, a modified Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) pipeline that replaces the standard three-channel RGB output head with a two-channel output. Complex-nerfacto represents the real and imaginary velocity components of a wavefield, preserving the complex measurement without quantization. Reconstructions of a welded aluminum cylinder and a welded T-bracket were evaluated against measured scans using Z-normalized cross-correlation (ZNCC). The complex-valued pipeline achieved a mean ZNCC of 0.60 at held-out viewing angles, compared with 0.28 for a baseline RGB nerfacto model trained on rendered images of the same data. The resulting surface wavefield reconstructions supported defect detection and characterization on complex components. We identify geometry reconstruction from sparse LDV scans as the remaining obstacle to practical deployment.

title: Content-Preserving Principal Feature Blending for Training-Free Style Personalization
summary: Reference-based style personalization should reproduce the appearance of a style reference while preserving the subject specified by a content prompt. In visual autoregressive models, dominant reference features can also carry object and spatial information, causing content leakage. We propose Content-Preserving Principal Feature Blending (CoPFB), a training-free method that estimates a low-rank content basis from a clean generation branch and removes the content-aligned component of the style residual. CoPFB applies rank-one blending at the first two autoregressive scales, followed by weaker content-projected refinement at the next three scales. On 1,900 combinations of Parti content prompts and FineStyle reference images, CoPFB improves text alignment from 0.293 to 0.297 and the harmonic score from 0.391 to 0.393 over PFB+SAC, while style similarity decreases from 0.590 to 0.577. CoPFB requires no fine-tuning or learnable parameters. Project page: https://vdkhoi20.github.io/CoPFB/.

title: S1CogBench: What System One Decision Models Can and Cannot Do on Cognitive Experiments
summary: Language models are no longer used only to generate text. Software also asks them for decisions, in routing, guardrails, and automated gates. System One decision models, also called typed decision models, such as Jev and Laya, return one fast decision over the legal options, leaving no text to inspect. However, a fast, well-formed decision does not show that the model used the evidence. Cognitive experiments can test this, because they vary task demands and measure how behavior changes, yet existing cognitive benchmarks evaluate language and multimodal models. We introduce S1CogBench to ask what these models can and cannot do on 24 cognitive tasks, evaluating five open models and Jev and keeping conditions and scoring apart from disclosed adaptations. We find that decision models vary widely in reliability, acting well does not imply predicting humans, aggregate scores hide how decisions respond to conditions, and speed comes mainly from answering without generation. To our knowledge, S1CogBench is the first benchmark of System One decision models on established cognitive experiments, and it gives a shared test of whether their decisions respond to evidence, feedback, memory load, and future opportunities before software relies on them.
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, 12 tables. Code at https://github.com/dengzhe-hou/S1CogBench

title: FastAgent: A Physics-Aware FastFluent-to-Fluent Workflow for Rapid CFD Screening and Industrial Steam Dewaxing Design
summary: Industrial computational fluid dynamics (CFD) becomes costly when complex geometries, long transients and coupled physics must be evaluated across large design spaces. We introduce FastAgent, a physics-aware campaign controller built around FastFluent, a lightweight numerical engine for rapid physical screening. FastFluent supplies stage-specific fields and diagnostics; FastAgent allocates physical models, numerical resolution and simulation horizons by the active quantities of interest (QoIs), while returned Fluent discrepancies update subsequent decisions. Across six public CFD benchmark campaigns, the framework reduces normalised worst-QoI error by 5.68-99.14% and accelerates decision-relevant computation by factors of 1.53-15.36 relative to a matched Generic Agent control. Applied to high-pressure steam dewaxing in investment casting, FastAgent identifies nonuniform condensation heating as the dominant startup mechanism and separates rapid risk-window localisation from high-fidelity melt-completion confirmation. The rapid route requires 81.39% fewer cell-time updates than a fine-grid, small-time-step reference. Structural analysis localises fracture at the observed blade edge. Screening 131,072 outlet layouts and selectively evaluating candidates with Fluent and Abaqus identifies Sparse-6, which reduces simulated crack opening by 96.0% and connected crack extent by 66.7% relative to the Original design. These results demonstrate how rapid numerical evidence and adaptive fidelity control connect large CFD search spaces to mechanism-guided industrial design.
comment: 47 pages, 6 main-text figures. Supplementary Information included

title: Minimum-Norm Interpolation in Weighted Variation Spaces: Direct and Inverse Problems
summary: We study minimum-norm interpolation in weighted variation spaces generated by ReLU$^s$ ridge functions on the unit ball, where $s$ is a positive integer. For a target $f$ in the weighted variation space and a node set with sufficiently small fill distance $h$, every minimum-norm interpolant satisfies the direct bound $\|f-\mathscr{I}_{X_h}f\|_{L_2(\mathbb{B}^d)}\lesssim_{d,s}h^{(2s+1)/4}\|f\|_{\mathcal{V}_s}$. Under a boundary separation condition on the nodes, we construct a matching lower bound for the worst-case interpolation error. For the inverse problem, we introduce dual certificates and derive an estimate analogous to a Bernstein inequality. Under suitable upper bounds on dictionary size and spectral lower bounds for the atomic Gram matrices, sufficiently fast $L_2$ convergence of minimum-norm interpolants along geometrically decreasing fill distances implies that the target belongs to $\mathcal{V}_s$. As a byproduct, the best $L_2$ approximation error $E_n(f)_{L_2(\mathbb{B}^d)}$ for shallow ReLU$^s$ networks of width at most $n$ satisfies $E_n(f)_{L_2(\mathbb{B}^d)}\lesssim_{d,s}n^{-1/2-(2s+1)/(2d)}\|f\|_{\mathcal{V}_s}$, with the weighted atomic cost of an approximating network bounded by a constant multiple of $\|f\|_{\mathcal{V}_s}$, independently of $n$.

title: Learned Surrogates of Three-Dimensional Magnetohydrodynamic Turbulence
summary: Three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence, the flow of astrophysical and fusion plasmas, is costly to simulate. We present, to our knowledge, the first learned surrogates of three-dimensional resistive MHD turbulence, and compare three standard backbones in that role: a convolutional UNet, a shifted-window transformer and a Fourier neural operator. They are trained as autoregressive emulators of decaying MHD turbulence at a resolution of $128^3$ and Reynolds numbers of 1000, 3000 and 6000, on 500 simulations per Reynolds number, each with one two-stage procedure, single steps and then short rollouts, and stopped by one rule. Over a window of about one large-eddy turnover time, the UNet and the transformer reach relative velocity errors of 0.018 to 0.053 and keep the current sheets, the enstrophy, the current density and the energy spectra of the simulation; which of the two is the more accurate depends on the Reynolds number, the UNet leading at 3000 and 6000 and the transformer at 1000. Applied with the same backbones and training procedure to two public benchmarks, the models reach the lowest error reported to date on the isotropic turbulence set of FactFormer, 39% below the best published model. On the compressible MHD set of The Well, their rollout errors are a third to a half below those of the best of The Well's baselines. They also match a 1.3 B-parameter pretrained foundation model in its rollout windows, with 20-62 times fewer parameters. The code, the configuration of every model, the evaluation scripts and the data generator with the seed of every simulation will be released upon publication.

title: Beyond Temporal Overlap: Consumer-Aware Evaluation of Sign-Language Segmentation across Three Corpora
summary: Sign-language segmentation divides continuous signing into clips. In this study, the downstream consumer is a frozen recognizer that assigns one sign label to each predicted clip. Existing metrics instead compare predicted clips with manually annotated boundaries. They do not directly measure whether a clip preserves the visual evidence needed by the recognizer or whether the segmenter produces too many clips. We therefore ask whether overlap metrics and this consumer prefer the same segmenter. We evaluate 27 outputs from three segmentation architectures, three random seeds, and three corpora. Controlled boundary edits separate the effect of removing sign evidence from that of adding surrounding context. Overlap predicts recognition on average, but it does not always determine model choice. At the same intersection-over-union, different recognizers can prefer the shorter or the longer clip. The real outputs reveal two operating regimes. On DGS, overlap, recognition, and sequence error select the same model. On BSL, recognition-based selection recovers and recognizes more reference signs but increases word error rate (WER). Dicta-Sign shows the reverse trade-off: WER selection reduces in-vocabulary WER by 31.17 points but misses more recognizable signs. Segmenters should therefore be evaluated on four axes: temporal agreement, reference recovery, clip recognition, and sequence error, rather than on overlap alone.
comment: Submitted to IEEE FG 2027. 9 pages, 4 figures. Supplementary material included

title: A Straight Line Is Not a Camera Pose: Auditing Short-Clip Pose Benchmarks
summary: The absolute trajectory error (ATE) is the standard measure of camera-motion accuracy, from SLAM to feed-forward 3D reconstruction. On the common Sintel protocol, a constant-velocity straight line using no images has a lower mean ATE than 10 of 11 recent models re-run with official code. Two properties of ATE's alignment explain this. First, it maps any constant-velocity prediction onto the best-fitting line through the true path, so the line scores the path's regression residual. A residual signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) criterion predicts when moving a prediction towards its constant-velocity fit lowers ATE. It gives the outcome for 95% of 1056 model-clip pairs, 98% of 792 held-out pairs and 97% of 1034 ScanNet pairs, and it separates Sintel (median SNR 0.86) from TUM, ScanNet and full-length Bonn and Wild-SLAM (2.7 to 27), where straightening raises every model's mean ATE. Second, position-only alignment ignores where cameras look: rotating a trajectory by 30 degrees against its orientations leaves ATE unchanged, yet worsens the reprojection of static points for every model on Sintel, TUM and ScanNet in the main setting, and the line, second by mean ATE on Sintel, places them worst by geometric mean: a lower ATE need not mean better geometry. Fitting the alignment's rotation to the predicted orientations gives pose-anchored ATE, a one-function change in ATE's units costing 0.17 ms per clip (ATE: 0.11 ms). It ranks every image-free reference below every model on Sintel, tracks the reprojection error under rotation and straightening, where ATE does not (Spearman 0.61 vs. 0.32), largely preserves the models' order, and ties 10-frame translational relative pose error (RPE) and the discernible trajectory error (DTE) on our rotation and reference tests. Code, predictions and results will be released.

title: Zero-Gated Cross-Attention
summary: Injecting non-text modalities into frozen language models often introduces early optimization instability, making it difficult to separate architectural gains from transient training dynamics. We introduce Inductively Gated Cross-Attention (IGCA), a zero-initialized cross-attention bridge that preserves pretrained model behavior at initialization while enabling gradual multimodal conditioning. Integrated across six decoder layers of frozen Falcon-40B, open_llama_30b, and Bloom-7b1 backbones (with 40,404,961,288 trainable adapter parameters used during training), IGCA acts as an exact algebraic no-op at initialization with a maximum output discrepancy of 0.00e+00. Over 59,500 training steps on Falcon-40B, the training loss decreases from 3.9403 to 0.0007 (with final ten step losses of [0.0001, 0.0003, 0.0005, 0.0002, 0.0005, 0.0011, 0.0005, 0.0006, 0.0005, 0.0007]). On held-out evaluation, the best gate-on checkpoint achieves a loss of 2.2201 compared to 4.3469 for the gate-off baseline -- a 48.9% reduction (2.1268 nats) -- while average held-out loss improves from 4.3423 to 2.2498 (1.9075 nats) with a mean gate magnitude of $\vert{}\tanh(α)\vert{} = 0.0713$.

title: SHield: Watermarking 4D Gaussian Splatting via Spherical Harmonic Coefficient Perturbation
summary: 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) models are computationally expensive to train but distributed as easily copied parameter files. Existing watermarks protect these assets by fine-tuning the scene against a neural decoder to extract bit strings from rendered video, a heavy process vulnerable to the temporal dynamics of dynamic scenes. However, if the threat model targets the redistributed file itself, verification can be vastly simplified. Because the canonical Spherical-Harmonic (SH) coefficients of 4DGS are time- and view-invariant, parameter-space perturbations can be recovered via deterministic arithmetic. We propose **SHield**, the first non-blind, decoder-free watermarking approach that natively embeds full-resolution RGB images into 4DGS files. SHield tiles a zero-mean payload across the SH coefficients of a key-selected Gaussian subset, applying a brief anchored optimization to preserve visual fidelity. To verify ownership, it geometrically re-associates the key using canonical Gaussian centres to survive file tampering and recovers the payload in closed form. Across 30 scenes (D-NeRF, HyperNeRF, DyNeRF), SHield guarantees near-perfect payload recovery (Pearson $r \geq 0.991$) on all 150 tested models with a mean rendering penalty of $\leq 0.13$~dB. Held-out evaluation yields perfect detection on 400 true trials and zero false positives across $1{,}600$ wrong-subset null trials. We also strictly bound the method's robustness: SHield survives INT8 quantization and $30\%$ opacity pruning for the image payload, and on aggressive SH-degree-1 truncation bit payloads are still decodable.

title: Bootstrap Inference for Riemannian Optimization Problems
summary: We develop an online multiplier bootstrap for manifold-valued parameters estimated by averaging the iterates of Riemannian stochastic approximation. The method runs weighted iterations alongside the original algorithm, with each path using the same observations while updating its own state and intrinsic average. The weighted averages provide uncertainty assessments without a plug-in asymptotic covariance estimator. Under local stability and regularity conditions, we establish bootstrap consistency and show that a fixed number of paths suffices for asymptotically valid Student intervals and intrinsic confidence regions. The theory accommodates samplewise nonsmooth scores and identifies a critical oracle-bias regime in which the estimator's limiting distribution shifts, but the centered bootstrap distribution does not. Applications include spherical means, positive-definite matrix means and medians, and principal-subspace estimation. Simulations show coverage close to nominal in regular settings, and an analysis of North Atlantic storm locations illustrates descriptive online inference for a spherical center.

title: Selective inference for pruned interaction trees with known unequal variances in randomized trials
summary: Interaction trees reuse outcomes to discover treatment-effect heterogeneity, complicating inference after growth and pruning. We develop selective inference for generalized least-squares (GLS) interaction trees with a common covariate basis and known unequal variances. Under a conditional Gaussian model with positive diagonal covariance, weighted orthogonality reduces survival under additive fixed-penalty pruning to one quadratic inequality supplementing the growth event. This yields exact finite-sample conditional tests and confidence intervals, with retained-path and complete-tree inference agreeing on compatible sections. Under causal identification and a correct reference prognosis, the pruning-invariant GLS target is a signed finite-design weighted contrast of conditional average treatment effects. Simulations at $n=100,200,400,800$ and maximum depths one to three search all adjacent-observation midpoints, support calibration and demonstrate over-rejection when pruning survival is omitted. Compared with a 50:50 honest procedure, full-data learning improves reference-split recovery in some small-sample settings. Root-level median intervals can be shorter, while deep-node intervals and upper tails can be much wider; these comparisons concern each procedure's selected targets. Estimating a common scale with the variance ratio fixed produces modest changes in Selective coverage in the settings examined, without extending the exact guarantee. An exploratory ACTG 175 analysis provides a working-model illustration with estimated arm variances.

title: CivicBench: A Benchmark and Memory Framework for Web-Based Civic Data Analytics
summary: Municipalities publish service requests, geographic boundaries, weather observations, demographic estimates, and operational guidance through independently maintained Web portals. Civic analysis must combine these sources while preserving their schemas, source links, spatial and temporal scopes, and interpretive limits. Tool-using language agents can perform this integration, but existing task benchmarks rarely test whether a computed claim remains supported by the records used. We present CivicBench, a 400-task benchmark over four cities and two years that materializes civic Web data into frozen bundles for reproducible evaluation. Executable contracts score computation, source linkage, coverage, scope, qualified answers, and refusal when the requested conclusion is not supported. We also introduce Task-State Memory (TSM), which compiles tool observations into typed assertions, reconciles records only within compatible scopes, and retrieves a bounded state organized around unresolved constraints. Across nine completed model pairs, eight yield positive mean-score differences with 95\% semantic-contract-cluster bootstrap intervals excluding zero; the ninth interval crosses zero. The benchmark and memory framework make the records behind a claim inspectable at the point of decision.

title: FilmTogether: Cinematic Video Generation from Low-Cost Inputs
summary: The widespread adoption of mobile devices has democratized video recording, but a stark aesthetic divide persists between casual, low-cost captures and high-cost cinematic productions. Bridging this gap requires upgrading heterogeneous production elements, such as lighting, specialized costumes, and materials, without altering the core layout, identity, and temporal motion of the original footage. However, this task is heavily bottlenecked by two important challenges: 1) Lacking a high-quality paired training data specifically designed to handle complex low-to-high appearance shifts. 2) Ignoring the capacity of current video editing models to perceive and enhance the multiple low-cost compositions. To address these issues, we present CineCraft-120K, a large-scale dataset of aligned low- and high-cost video pairs annotated with pair-aware editing prompts. CineCraft-120K features a diverse, high-resolution and high-cost Cinematic Crafting bank spanning decades of media production, meticulously taxonomized into 5 broad domains and 23 fine-grained sub-categories. It also provides element-level mapping between low- and high-cost counterparts, offering pair-aware rich textual prompts that precisely detail the required aesthetic transformations while anchoring structural layout. Architecturally, we propose a simple yet effective dual-memory feature adapter, where a text-memory expands semantic capacity for low2high appearance changes, and a hint memory supplies layer-wise visual feature corrections of high-cost element before context injection. Extensive experiments and ablation studies demonstrate the superiority of CineCraft-120K for low-to-high-cost video editing, alongside the effectiveness of our dual-memory adapter.

title: Label Smoothing in Disguise? Gated Knowledge Distillation for Low-Resource Bangla Generation
summary: Gated knowledge distillation (KD) weights teacher signals per token or example, aiming to trust an imperfect teacher only where it seems reliable. We test two gates: EWAD (entropy-weighted agreement-aware distillation), which gates tokens by teacher confidence, and CHAD (counterfactual harm-aware distillation), which gates examples by gradient alignment with validation data. Across six Bangla-centric tasks, three student models (60M to about 2B parameters), and two teacher families, no gate significantly improves plain KD in 45 comparisons. KD also fails to beat cross-entropy (CE) fine-tuning on gold outputs in 40 single-seed comparisons or three-seed runs on four tasks; CE leads on every summarisation metric. The main benefit of KD is regularisation: over ten fixed epochs, CE students lose 0.030 to 0.044 token-F1 from their early-stopped checkpoint, versus 0.005 to 0.025 for distilled students. Teacher-free label smoothing closes most of this gap. In one comparison, a teacher 0.29 token-F1 worse yields students at most 0.009 worse. Thus, gating may change regularisation strength but has little teacher knowledge to select. Findings are limited to Bangla-centric tasks and small students. We will release code, data splits, predictions, and scores.

title: Heirloom: Carrying a Phone's Personalization Across Base-Model Generations
summary: On-device language models can learn a user's preferences through adapters trained on private data. However, a base-model upgrade may change the layers or vocabulary, leaving the personal adapter incompatible. Replacing it with a non-personal adapter loses much of the personalization, while retraining requires retaining the user's labeled history. We present Heirloom, a system that transfers a personal adapter to a new base model on the phone without retaining labels. Heirloom uses the old personal model as a teacher, collecting its predictions on stored unlabeled inputs, vendor-provided prompts, or prompts generated by the new base. It then unloads the old base and trains an adapter for the new model to match those predictions, keeping only one base model in memory at a time. We evaluate Heirloom across three generation upgrades from two model families, an architecture-preserving refresh, and three personalization tasks. On movie tagging, migration from stored inputs maintains pre-upgrade accuracy and differs from labeled retraining by at most 1.7 percentage points across the three upgrades. On a phone's neural processing unit (NPU), a fixed-length migration for the 4B upgrade takes 38 minutes and consumes 20% of the battery end to end, making the stored-input setting feasible during overnight charging.

title: Fewer Tokens, More Answers: Verifiable-Reward Tuning of an Ornith-Style VLM for Multi-View Driving QA
summary: Reasoning-enabled model derivatives must turn intermediate deliberation into a usable answer within a deployment budget. We study that transition in an Ornith checkpoint adapted to multi-camera driving question answering with verifiable rewards. Paired archived outputs show that, on a selected 400-question development screen with a 256-token cap, GRPO increases answer extraction from 78.25% to 90.25% and accuracy from 55.50% to 63.75%. Of 39 wrong-to-correct transitions, 33 begin with an unextractable base response. The base's 87 unextractable responses all reach the token cap. Checkpoint-verified reconstruction on those same questions gives a much smaller first-pass accuracy gain at 512 tokens: +0.75 percentage points, versus +8.25 at 256. A later answer-cued continuation is analyzed separately; it helps the base more and narrows the adapter difference. On the full 2,511-question development set, this recovery-enabled pipeline reduces mean generated tokens from 108.6 to 47.1, while the paired accuracy interval includes zero gain. We frame these findings as adaptation of answer delivery under finite budgets, with explicit selection and provenance limits. Ornith's self-scaffolding lineage and newer reasoning-enabled derivatives such as Bonsai motivate the problem, but our measured results concern Ornith alone and do not establish a shared architectural mechanism or cross-model transfer.

title: Can Jev Improve Demonstration Retrieval for In-Context Learning?
summary: Demonstration selection plays a crucial role in the effectiveness of in-context learning (ICL) for large language models (LLMs). Extensive research has explored various retrieval strategies to identify informative demonstrations and improve downstream performance. Recently, the emergence of Jev, a decision-oriented language model capable of producing probabilistic judgments, offers a new perspective on evaluating demonstration utility. This motivates us to investigate a fundamental question: Can Jev improve demonstration retrieval for in-context learning? In this paper, we demonstrate that Jev can effectively enhance demonstration retrieval by directly assessing the utility of candidate demonstrations for a given query. However, applying Jev to large-scale retrieval introduces substantial computational overhead, as each candidate requires an additional decision-making inference. To address this limitation, we propose a simple yet effective knowledge distillation approach that transfers Jev's utility estimation capability to a lightweight multilayer perceptron (MLP). By learning to approximate Jev's probabilistic judgments, the distilled model enables efficient demonstration ranking while maintaining competitive retrieval performance. Our study highlights the potential of decision-oriented language models for demonstration selection and provides an efficient framework for integrating their decision-making capabilities into ICL.

title: datasette-llm 0.1a9
summary: Release: datasette-llm 0.1a9 I have some big upgrades to Datasette Agent in the pipeline, but in the meantime here's a tiny user experience improvement to the underlying datasette-llm plugin. It now picks up the default model used by LLM , which means you can start using Datasette Agent without needing to explicitly configure a default model: uvx --with datasette-agent datasette content.db --internal internal.db Previously you would also need to specify a model with -s plugins.datasette-agent.default_model gpt-6-astra .
